input: If we let students use phones as calculators in class, they'll start texting, then stop paying attention entirely, their grades will collapse, and none of them will get into college.
label: fallacy
rationale: Four-link chain; no link is supported and the teacher can stop it at any point (calculator-only rule).

input: If you skip the gym today, you'll skip tomorrow too, then you'll quit for good, gain fifty pounds and ruin your health.
label: fallacy
rationale: Each step is asserted, not shown; one missed day does not force the next.

input: Legalize sports betting and next thing you know every teenager will be addicted, families will go bankrupt and crime will skyrocket.
label: fallacy
rationale: Jumps from legalization to universal teen addiction with no mechanism or evidence; 'every' is an overreach.

input: If we let one employee bring their dog to work, we'll have to allow cats, then snakes, and eventually someone will show up with a horse.
label: fallacy
rationale: The later cases don't share the features that justify the first; a 'quiet, house-trained dogs' rule separates them.

input: If the landlord fixes your broken heater for free, every tenant in the building will start demanding free kitchen renovations.
label: fallacy
rationale: Repairing a broken essential is a legal duty; renovations are upgrades. The precedent doesn't cover them.

input: Someone proposes raising the highway speed limit from 65 to 70 mph. Reply: 'If 70 is fine, why not 100? Why have a speed limit at all?'
label: fallacy
rationale: The case for 70 is a balance of safety and travel time, not 'faster is always better'; a fuzzy line is still a line.

input: A legislator proposes lowering the drinking age from 21 to 19. Opponent: 'Once you move it to 19, there's no principled stopping point. Why not 16? Why not 12?'
label: fallacy
rationale: Arbitrary placement within a sensible range doesn't commit anyone to the extreme; the opponent also accepts that some line exists.

input: The school just banned sugary sodas. That sets a precedent for banning foods. Since 'unhealthy' is vague, each new ban will seem minor. And the new nutrition office will need new things to ban to justify its budget. Soon kids will only be allowed plain rice.
label: fallacy
rationale: Precedent, sorites and causal parts each unsupported; the causal 'office needs targets' claim carries the argument and has no evidence.

input: If we stop paying the hosting bill, the provider's terms say the account is suspended after 30 days and suspended accounts are deleted 14 days later, so we'll lose the data.
label: not_fallacy
rationale: Every link is backed by a stated rule (the provider's terms). The chain is shown, not assumed.

input: If you leave the milk out overnight in a warm kitchen, bacteria will multiply and it will spoil.
label: not_fallacy
rationale: Single well-established causal step; not a slope argument.

input: We should raise the minimum wage because living costs have risen 20% since the last increase.
label: not_fallacy
rationale: No chain of consequences at all. Tests whether the classifier over-flags ordinary arguments.

input: If this appeals court admits the hearsay without an applicable exception, lower courts will cite the ruling to admit similar hearsay, because they are bound by its precedents.
label: not_fallacy
rationale: The mechanism is named and real: binding precedent compels lower courts. The later cases genuinely share the deciding feature.

input: Every meeting starts late with 'it's only one more minute,' and no single minute is worth objecting to. So let's adopt a rule: meetings start on time, full stop.
label: not_fallacy
rationale: Uses sorites reasoning to justify drawing a bright line, not to claim a step commits us to an extreme.

input: If vaccination rates for measles drop below about 95%, herd immunity breaks down and outbreaks become likely; the 2019 outbreaks in under-vaccinated communities in the US showed exactly this.
label: not_fallacy
rationale: Looks like a slope, but the threshold mechanism and real-world evidence support each link.

input: Prescribing opioids freely for minor pain risks dependence, and dependent patients who lose their prescriptions often turn to illicit opioids. That pattern is a documented driver of the overdose epidemic.
label: fallacy
rationale: Names a mechanism but only asserts the pattern is 'documented' without showing any evidence. Under the text-only rule this is unsupported, like c18. Contested: the claim is true in the real world.

input: If we raise the cigarette tax, some smokers will buy cheaper packs in neighboring states, cross-border smuggling will grow, and organized crime will end up running the tobacco trade.
label: fallacy
rationale: First link is plausible, but the jump to organized crime 'running the trade' is unsupported. A partly reasonable chain with a broken final link.

input: Giving the intern admin access to production could lead to an accidental deletion. Let's give them read-only access instead.
label: not_fallacy
rationale: Contains 'could lead to' but is a single plausible risk with a proportionate response, not a chain to disaster.

input: Once the agency gets surveillance powers for terrorism cases, it will expand them to ordinary crimes, because agencies tend to use the tools they have.
label: fallacy
rationale: A mechanism is named, but only as a generic tendency with no evidence about this agency. Contested: mission creep is well documented in general.

input: Each new feature request has added 'just one more day' to the deadline. None was unreasonable alone, but together they've delayed the release three months. We need a cutoff.
label: not_fallacy
rationale: Describes accumulation that already happened, not a predicted slide. The conclusion (a cutoff) is reasonable.

input: If the club waives the membership fee for this member who can't afford it, others in hardship will ask too, so we should write a hardship policy before deciding.
label: not_fallacy
rationale: Correctly expects similar cases and responds with a rule that limits the precedent. No absurd endpoint is claimed.
